extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of English literature and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the rhetorical, stylistic, thematic, and structural techniques that make a satirical essay (exemplified by Swift's A Modest Proposal) effective or notable. Useful for literary analysis and for writers aiming to produce sustained, ironical satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained irony
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay is 'one of the greatest examples of sustained irony' in English literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent ironic distance between the narrator's apparent advocacy and the author's true stance so the reader gradually recognizes the inversion. The shock/value often comes from keeping the ironic posture over an extended argument rather than as a brief joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock through surprise juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of its shock value derives from describing the plight of starving beggars first so the reader is unprepared for the surprise solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish empathetic or serious context before proposing an outrageous remedy; the contrast amplifies satirical impact (e.g., describing poverty in detail before proposing cannibalistic 'solutions').

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan / serious tone (proposer's earnestness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses a 'deadpan' or serious tone — the proposer's serious tone highlights the absurdity of his proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a calm, rational voice when stating absurd claims; the mismatch between tone and content produces dark humour and forces readers to evaluate the underlying values being mocked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a fictional narrator/persona
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay is 'written from the perspective of a fictional narrator' (the Proposer) whose views are distinct from the author's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a clearly authored persona whose social position and values are subject to critique; ensure the text creates a gap between narratorial attitude and the author's apparent moral stance so readers can detect the satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralipsis / apophasis to suggest real reforms indirectly
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduces the reforms Swift actually suggests by paralipsis (apophasis): listing alternatives like taxing absentee landlords, buying Irish goods, improving treatment of tenants, then dismissing them to highlight the absurdity of the main proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paralipsis to name sensible policies while ostensibly rejecting them, forcing the reader to infer the true recommendations. This indirectness can sharpen critique by contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lampooning contemporary 'social engineering' and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Lampoons the then-influential William Petty and the social engineering popular among Francis Bacon's followers; mocks projects that offered simple cure-all solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target specific popular intellectual fashions or authorities of your time and mimic their language/logic in an exaggerated way to expose their folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faux-mathematical/statistical argument (political arithmetician technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopts the 'technique of a political arithmetician' — includes 'calculations showing the financial benefits' to give a veneer of dispassionate, faux-scientific justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pseudo-statistics, cost–benefit arithmetic, and cold numerical reasoning to satirize utilitarian and technocratic approaches; the apparent rigor makes the immorality or absurdity more striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dehumanizing vocabulary / animal husbandry metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker uses 'the vocabulary of animal husbandry' to describe the Irish, turning 'people into animals, then meat'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dehumanizing metaphors deliberately through the persona to expose the logic of commodification; let the reader see how language reduces persons to units of economic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative appeals for ironic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to authority ironically (e.g., 'a very knowing American of my acquaintance in London' and 'the famous Psalmanazar').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dubious or irrelevant appeals to 'experts' to parody credulous reliance on authority; the more plausible the appeal appears, the sharper the satire when the claim is absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical rhetorical structure (Quintilian-derived argument order)
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker uses the 'conventional, textbook-approved order of argument' derived from Quintilian, contrasting careful form with perverse content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic formal rhetorical structures to lend a veneer of respectability to immoral or absurd claims; the formal correctness amplifies the critique by showing how respectable forms can be used for perverse ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical 'trap' to manipulate reader sympathy and disgust
rubrics_metrics.description: Swift's rhetorical strategy uses a 'trap' to create sympathy for the Irish and a dislike of the narrator by alternating vivid poverty details with the narrator's detached attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate emotional appeals (gripping detail) with unemotional argumentation by the persona so readers feel conflicted and are led to repudiate the persona's values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap between narrator's apparent meaning and the text's moral-political argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must 'distinguish between the satirical voice of Jonathan Swift and the apparent economic projections of the Proposer' — there is a 'gap between the narrator's meaning and the text's'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the text so the surface argument can be plausibly read at face value while the broader context, tone, and contrasts reveal the author's critical intention; allow attentive readers to infer the ethical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burlesque/parody of policy proposals and poor-relief projects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Modest Proposal is described as 'a burlesque of projects concerning the poor' — parodying fashionable schemes like joint-stock approaches to poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate the form and rhetoric of real policy proposals to where they become grotesque; use parody of procedural details to reveal hidden assumptions and cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with contemporary economic and political themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets ideas such as mercantilism, regressive tax legislation, absentee landlords, and the mercantilist maxim that 'people are the riches of a nation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor satire in recognizable political/economic debates so the critique reads as topical and purposeful; showing intimate knowledge of contemporaneous theories strengthens the burlesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juvenalian satire qualities: wit, dark humour, and moral indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified as 'one of the most prominent works of Juvenalian satire' and acclaimed for its 'wit, satire and dark humour' addressing 'social injustice, poverty and class dehumanisation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ bitter, abrasive, and morally serious tones (Juvenalian mode) rather than playful Horatian mockery when the aim is to condemn social evils rather than merely amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid, concrete detail to dramatize suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses 'gripping details of poverty' to force the reader to see the human cost before the ironic twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sensory, specific depictions of harm to ground the satire ethically and emotionally; concrete detail makes later rhetorical manipulations more morally provocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast of controlled form and perverse content to reveal underlying values
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'contrast between the "careful control against the almost inconceivable perversion of his scheme" and "the ridiculousness of the proposal"' makes readers consider the perverted values that enable such a plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the argument methodical and seemingly reasonable while presenting morally perverse conclusions so readers must interrogate the assumptions and values that permit such logic.
